Clear authority.

"How many workers?"

"Depends day. Around twenty across all three crews."

Not my twenty.

Important.

"What are fields doing?"

"Seasonal drainage and late-cut cleanup before wet turn. Ditch clearing. Cut brush. Pull old stakes. Reset access paths. Some bundling. No crop judgment from organizer."

Better.

"Fee?"

She slid a sheet across table.

**ORGANIZER TERM / FOUR DAYS**

**6S ON ACCEPTED START PLAN + CONFIRMED CREW/TRANSPORT CONTACTS**

**12S ON COMPLETION OF FOUR-DAY HANDOFF IF ALL DAILY ORGANIZER RECORDS ACCEPTED**

**NO COMPLETION FEE IF ORGANIZER ABANDONS TERM WITHOUT HOUSE RELEASE**

**HOUSE COVERS AUTHORIZED MESSAGE / RECORD / LOCAL CART COSTS**

Eighteen silver total.

I read again.

Actually silver.

More importantly, I was not being paid to clear a ditch.

I was being paid so twenty people and several moving parts did not waste four days.

"What counts accepted record?"

"Start roster. Actual arrival. Section assignment. Tool issue discrepancies. Cart delay. Work handoff. Anything house steward marks relevant. Not a diary."

"What if crew lead changes sequence for field reason?"

"You record it and adjust shared schedule."

"What if I disagree?"

"If it's field method, you don't matter."

I liked her.

"References required."

I gave both.

She read Rinna first.

Longer than I expected.

Then Antonius.

She looked at me.

"You owe Vale?"

"Yes."

"How much?"

"I haven't reconciled the whole account recently. Enough that I should."

"Does this job require you to front house expenses?"

"Sheet says no."

"Good."

No shame.

Just risk.

"Why field crews?"

"Because notice existed."

"Bad answer."

"Because I spent a long time thinking useful work meant personally doing task. Recently I have been more useful connecting people and keeping separate expertise aligned. I wanted to know if that transfers to more people."

She watched me.

"That's a speech."

"Unfortunately."

"Shorter."

I thought.

"I think I can keep three competent crews from waiting on the same cart."

There.

She nodded once.

"Better."

Interview continued.

Not dramatic.

She gave scenarios.

Two crews arrive, third late.

Water cart missing.

Field steward closes lower section.

One crew lead wants to borrow tools issued to another crew.

Contract wagon leaves early because driver claims route changed.

I did not solve everything brilliantly.

On tool borrowing I said organizer could reassign.

Wrong.

"Tool keeper owns issue."

Right.

On closed field I initially moved crew immediately.

She asked whether alternate section was ready.

I had not checked.

Good.

On late crew I said start others if their work independent.

Correct enough.

On missing water cart I asked whether work could begin safely without it.

"Field steward decides."

Right.

On wagon I asked who contracted it and what written route term said.

That got a tiny nod.

At end she said, "You are not first choice."

Good.

"Who is?"

"Woman who did spring turn. She is north with family."

"Second?"

"Man from Miller Lane. He wants hiring authority we are not giving him."

Interesting.

"So?"

"You can have provisional term if references verify today. Start plan due by first bell tomorrow. If plan accepted, six silver. If first morning goes badly enough, house can release you and you keep only accepted-plan payment."

"Fair."

"Don't say fair until you read whole term."

Antonius disease.

I read whole term.

Four pages.

Not exciting.

Useful.

No hidden worker wage liability.

No requirement I guarantee attendance.

No authority to discipline crews.

House could release for material organizer failure.

I could withdraw before start plan acceptance with no fee and no penalty.

After start, abandoning without release forfeited completion fee.

No invented fine.

I signed.

She signed for field office.

"Now references."

She sent a runner.

House expense.

I waited.

Luxury again.

Rinna's answer returned first.

Confirmed.

Antonius's second.

Confirmed.

The woman at table handed me a packet.

Crew contact sheets.

Three leads, names on paper.

I did not need their names in my head yet.

Better categories first.

North crew.

Middle crew.

Lower crew.

Each had meet point, expected headcount range, tool needs already agreed, and one note from prior organizer.

North crew liked to start early and hated waiting for carts.

Middle crew had one older worker who carried their own ditch gauge.

Lower crew had two workers joining only second day.

Not problems.

Facts.

Transport sheet:

Cart A water and meal.

Cart B tools and spoil baskets.

Contract wagon for cut brush from lower turnout afternoon only.

Field sections:

North ditch.

Middle access line.

Lower drainage cut.

I asked for map.

She gave one.

I asked for current readiness.

"Field steward checks at dusk."

"Can I see results?"

"Posted here after sixth bell."

Good.

I spent rest of afternoon meeting crew leads.

Not recruiting.

Not motivational speech.

Just contact.

North crew lead was a compact woman with mud dried to one boot and no patience for introductions.

"You organizer?"

"Provisional."

"Can you make carts arrive?"

"No."

She stared.

"Can you tell me before they don't?"

"Sometimes."

"Better."

Good relationship start.

Middle crew lead talked too much.

A lot too much.

He explained, without apparent need for air, that his people could clear ditch, path, old stake, light brush, medium brush, some heavy brush if the roots were not stonebound, but they were absolutely not hauling wet spoil uphill again because last season somebody had called that "temporary repositioning" and temporary had lasted three hours and two backs and one argument with a mule.

I let him finish.

"Wet spoil uphill is not in your sheet."

"Good."

"If it appears?"

"We discuss before anybody decides language changes weight."

Excellent.

Lower crew lead was formal.

"Our contracted headcount on first day is six. Second day may be eight. I will confirm at evening bell. We require the two long-handled ditch hooks listed. If unavailable, I prefer reassignment before substitution."

"Because?"

"Short hooks change body position."

"Understood. Tool keeper owns issue. I'll flag availability, not invent replacement."

He nodded.

Different speech.

Different people.

By sixth bell I returned field office.

Dusk readiness sheet posted.

North ditch: **READY**.

Middle access line: **READY**.

Lower drainage cut: **HOLD / WATER STILL HIGH / RECHECK FIRST LIGHT**.

There.

Plan changed before plan existed.

Original packet assumed north, middle, lower start together.

Could assign lower crew elsewhere temporarily.

But alternate work needed readiness.

I asked field steward.

Unnamed man with coat tied around waist and mud to knees.

"If lower still held at first light, what work can that crew legally start?"

"North spoil bundling after north crew clears first hundred pace. Or old-stake pull on middle south edge."

"Which creates least interference?"

"Depends pace."

"Can lower lead choose at start based on actual progress?"

"Yes, if I approve section."

Good.

So plan did not force one.

It created decision point.

I wrote:

**FIRST BELL**

North crew -> North ditch.

Middle crew -> Middle access line.

Lower crew -> report Lower Gate, hold assignment until field-steward first-light status.

If lower cut opens -> Lower drainage.

If still closed -> steward selects North bundling or Middle old-stake edge based on readiness; lower crew lead owns work method.

Cart A -> water/meal first North turnout, then Middle, then Lower Gate hold point unless steward redirects.

Cart B -> tool issue at Lower Gate before crews split; long ditch hooks reserved to Lower crew only if lower drainage opens, otherwise remain tool-keeper custody.

Contract wagon -> lower turnout afternoon only, confirm after first-light lower status.

Then communication.

One runner token to North turnout.

One to Middle.

Field office runner held for wagon notice if lower status changes.

I did not need people sprinting because I had failed to decide where information moved.

That felt old.

Not old life exactly.

Old reflex.

I took plan home.

Lyssa was eating over work table.

Bad sign.

"You got job?"

"Provisional organizer term."

She looked up.

"Organizer."

"Apparently."

"People?"

"Around twenty."

She stopped chewing.

I enjoyed that too much.

"You are in charge of twenty people?"

"No."

"Good."

"Three crew leads are in charge of their crews. Field steward owns field decisions. Tool keeper owns tools. Office owns pay. I own schedule and shared failure."

"Shared failure."

"Strong title."

"How much?"

"Six silver if they accept start plan. Twelve more after four-day handoff if records accepted."

She did math with face.

"Eighteen silver."

"Yes."

"And if you don't ruin crops, the term actually matters."

I looked at her.

"There are no crops in my authority."

"You know what I mean."

I did.

Eighteen silver total.

A different tier from the copper jobs I had been stacking.

If.

Not mine yet.

Important.

"Six first," I said.

"Good."

She went back to eating.

"Also drainage."

"Less romantic."

"Much."

I slept badly because apparently management had discovered anticipation.

First bell came cold and gray.

I reached Lower Gate early.

Two crutches.

Shoulder bag.

Plan.

No trial leg.

No magic.

I was not walking fields if I could avoid it.

Organizer did not mean personally inspecting every ditch.

Field steward arrived with first-light status.

Lower drainage cut: **HOLD**.

Water had dropped, not enough.

Good.

Plan branch B.

Then Cart B did not arrive.

Of course.

North crew arrived.

Middle crew arrived.

Lower crew arrived with six.

No tools.

One cart missing.

Cart A water and meal was there.

I checked time.

Then asked field office.

Cart B axle pin broken three streets north.

Repair underway.

Estimated half bell.

Maybe.

North crew lead said, "We have our hand tools. We need baskets later."

Middle lead began a long explanation about how his crew technically had enough hooks to start but not enough spare handles if one cracked and one always cracked when somebody said there were enough handles.

Lower lead said, "Without long hooks, lower cut is irrelevant. For alternate old-stake work we have personal pry bars."

There.

Capability distributed.

I asked field steward.

"Can lower crew start middle south-edge stake pull now?"

He looked at Middle lead.

"If your crew stays north half until second bell."

Middle lead inhaled for speech.

I raised hand.

"Can you?"

He stopped.

"Yes."

"Then lower takes south-edge stakes until Cart B arrives or lower drainage opens."

Lower lead nodded.

North crew lead said, "We're starting."

"Yes."

They left.

No applause.

Good.

I sent one runner to Cart B repair point for update.

House token.

Then Cart A driver said his route sheet listed Lower first.

My plan said North first.

Old version.

There it was.

Different versions.

Theatre again.

I showed signed start plan.

Driver showed route sheet from yesterday.

Neither of us wrong.

Office had failed update.

I did not yell.

Growth.

"Can you run North first without breaking your cart agreement?"

"Agreement says field office route."

"Then office can correct."

We walked five yards to table.

Office woman wrote amended route.

Driver signed receipt.

North first.

Problem gone.

Not heroic.

Useful.

By second bell, North ditch was moving.

Middle access line moving.

Lower crew pulling old stakes and complaining that whoever drove them last year had hated future generations.

Cart B arrived after repair.

Tool keeper checked pin before releasing cart onward.

Not me.

Good.

Field steward rechecked lower water.

Still hold.

So long hooks stayed with tool keeper.

No reason to issue them just because packet said Lower crew.

By third bell, the lower crew had cleared enough old stakes that Middle lead wanted south edge early.

Conflict.

Not fight.

Timing.

I asked both leads what they needed.

Middle lead gave six sentences.

Lower lead gave two.

Result: lower could finish current thirty paces, then move to North spoil bundling. Middle could expand south afterward.

Field steward approved.

Done.

At midday I realized I had not eaten.

Bad management.

Of self.

I took meal from house issue like everyone else entitled by contract.

Sat on overturned basket near gate.

Hands tired from crutches and paper.

Right leg fine.

Shoulder ordinary.

No magic fatigue because I had not done anything stupid.

North crew lead passed with water cup.

"Cart came."

"I noticed."

"You told us before it came."

"That was goal."

"Good."

Then she left.

That was probably more satisfying than praise should have been.

By fourth bell, field office woman called me over.

She had my start plan.

Marked in three places.

"Accepted."

Six silver on table.

There.

Not completion.

Not eighteen.

Six.

I counted once.

She said, "Your actual-arrival record is missing Cart A route correction time."

I looked.

She was right.

I had written amendment, not time.

"Fix."

I did.

"Also lower crew alternate assignment changed at second bell. Record who approved."

"Field steward."

"Write it."

I did.

"You're doing fine."

Dangerous sentence.

I waited.

"That does not mean relax."

There.

Safer.

"Three more days."

"Yes."

"Completion fee is not earned."

"I know."

"Good."

I put six silver away.

Operating reserve intact.

Twelve more silver still conditional.

Closer.

Not there.

At fifth bell the lower drainage finally opened.

Too late to move crew there productively that day.

Field steward said tomorrow first bell.

Lower lead agreed.

Middle lead had opinions about whether lower water would rise overnight based on cloud shape, ditch smell, one frog, and his grandmother.

Field steward listened politely.

Then said, "We check at first light."

Hessa would have approved.

I did not tell anyone.

At close I wrote actual day state.

North: ditch clear through marked section, spoil bundling partly done.

Middle: access line clear through north half, south-edge stakes partly cleared by Lower crew before handoff.

Lower: drainage closed until fifth bell, no drainage work performed, alternate stake work completed in bounded section.

Cart A: old route sheet corrected at first bell plus.

Cart B: delayed by axle pin repair, arrived before second bell plus.

No worker injuries reported to organizer.

No claim that none existed outside reports.

Tool keeper retained long hooks.

Contract wagon not called because lower brush haul did not start.

Tomorrow: lower drainage only if steward opens at first light.

There.

Not a victory.

A current state.

I knew this feeling.

Old life before a fight when everyone had different capabilities, different timing, and enough ego to make geometry political.

But this was not battle.

Nobody was dying.

Nobody needed buff timing.

Nobody needed me to make them stronger.

They needed water in right place.

Tools not issued to wrong crew.

A cart route updated before driver left.

A field held because water was high.

Three leads allowed to remain better at their jobs than me.

Support without power.

I almost wrote that.

Did not.

Too neat.

Instead I wrote:

**Organizer day 1: plan is not instruction to reality. Plan is shared version until reality changes. Keep authority attached to person who can actually decide.**

Still a little neat.

Fine.

At home Lyssa was not there yet.

Her work had its own schedule.

Good.

I put six new silver beside the rest.

Not eighteen silver for the term.

Not yet.

Twelve completion silver sat in someone else's future obligation, contingent on three more days and acceptable records.

I did not count it.

Growth.

Then I looked at Antonius's reference again.

**reads terms before agreeing more often than he used to**

Rude.

Accurate.

Tomorrow lower field might flood again.

A crew might come short.

Cart B might break something more expensive than a pin.

Middle lead might explain weather to death.

None of that belonged to me yet.

What belonged to me was current state, current scope, and next bell.

For once, that was enough management.
# CHAPTER 486

## THE COORDINATOR

Day two was mostly boring.

That was excellent.

I had spent enough of my life around people who believed competent coordination should look dramatic.

Usually dramatic coordination meant somebody had failed earlier.

South Road did not need me dramatically.

It needed three crews, two carts, one contracted wagon, a field steward, a tool keeper, an office, and several pieces of paper to keep agreeing about what was happening.

That was harder than it sounded.

It was also less interesting to watch.

North crew started early.

Middle crew started almost early.

Lower drainage opened after first light and stayed open.

Cart A followed the corrected route.

Cart B arrived with both long ditch hooks.

The contract wagon appeared when promised.

Nobody cheered.

I loved everyone.

At second bell the North lead told me their spoil-basket count was wrong by three.

I checked my sheet.

My sheet said twelve.

Her crew had nine.

“Tool keeper?”

“Already told.”

“Then why tell me?”

“So you stop writing twelve.”

Fair.

I changed twelve to nine and added the time.

That was coordination.

Not fixing baskets.

Not finding baskets.

Not asking why baskets had betrayed us.

Current state.

At third bell Middle lead found me near the access line and spent enough words to irrigate a field.

“The south edge is technically open, and when I say technically I mean someone has cut the top brush and declared victory while leaving three root crowns, one buried stone, and a section of old ditch wall exactly where every reasonable person will put a foot. So yes, I can send people there. No, I will not send people there while somebody calls it clear, because if I hear the phrase mostly clear one more time I am going to start applying mostly to other nouns. Mostly fed. Mostly paid. Mostly alive.”

I waited.

He breathed.

“Field steward?”

“Coming.”

“Good.”

Field steward came.

Looked.

Said south edge was not ready.

Middle crew stayed where it was.

I changed the sheet.

Nothing else happened.

Beautiful.

At lunch I ate sitting on an overturned basket because chairs were a city conspiracy.

The North lead passed, looked at my notebook, and said, “Still alive?”

“Against projections.”

“Whose?”

“Mine.”

She kept walking.

Day two ended with no missing workers, no wrong cart, no section hold after start, and only one meal count correction because Lower crew actually had eight that day instead of six.

I did not solve that either.

Lower lead had confirmed eight at evening bell as promised.

I had failed to update meal count before Cart A loaded.

That was mine.

Not disaster.

Still mine.

The field office sent two additional meal portions on the next local cart.

Authorized house cost.

I wrote:

**DAY TWO ERROR: headcount confirmation updated roster, not provisioning count. Same fact existed in two places. I changed one.**

That annoyed me.

Useful.

The office woman read the line at end of day.

“You like writing your own mistakes.”

“No.”

“You do it often.”

“That is different.”

She marked the daily record accepted.

No money.

Correct.

Completion fee lived in future.

The six-silver start payment stayed in reserve with the rest of my working money.

Third day started clean.

Which should have frightened me.

North had ten.

Middle seven.

Lower eight.

Twenty-five total that morning.

More than first day.

Still not mine.

Crew leads had people.

House had contract.

I had shared state.

Cart A water and meal.

Cart B tools and baskets.

Contract wagon lower turnout after third bell to haul cut brush.

Lower drainage remained open.

Middle south edge finally cleared.

North ditch had moved far enough that their spoil bundling no longer interfered with Lower alternate work.

Everything fit.

Then field office changed priority.

A runner found me just before second bell.

Folded note.

Stamped by field office.

**HOUSE PRIORITY CHANGE**

**CONTRACT WAGON AFTER THIRD BELL: NORTH TURNOUT FIRST. CLEAR NORTH BRUSH STACK BEFORE EVENING HOUSE CART PASSAGE. LOWER TURNOUT AFTER NORTH IF TIME.**

There.

Real instruction.

Not rumor.

Not driver memory.

Not somebody shouting over a ditch.

Field office stamp.

I read twice.

North turnout first.

Lower after if time.

This was inconvenient because Lower crew had been cutting and bundling based on the wagon arriving at their turnout after third bell.

I looked at current board.

Contract wagon line.

Lower turnout.

Crossed it out.

Wrote North first.

Sent runner token to North.

Sent one to contract wagon meet point.

Updated field office copy when I passed.

Good.

Very efficient.

Very wrong.

I did not tell Lower.

Not immediately.

That was the mistake.

It took almost half a bell to become visible.

I was at Middle checking whether their south-edge handoff had been recorded when Lower lead appeared.

He did not hurry.

That made it worse.

“Our wagon has been reassigned.”

“Yes.”

“To North.”

“Yes.”

“Since before second bell.”

I looked at him.

There it was.

“You were not told.”

“No.”

“I changed the route and sent notice to wagon and North.”

“I noticed.”

His voice stayed formal.

Not loud.

“You did not send notice to the crew whose work plan depended on the wagon you removed.”

Correct.

I hated him.

“Correct.”

“We continued cutting brush for the lower haul.”

“How much?”

“Enough that the turnout is now becoming inconvenient.”

Not dangerous.

Not disaster.

Still a problem.

“Why didn’t you stop when wagon didn’t arrive?”

“It is not after third bell.”

Right.

They were still working under valid old schedule.

The wagon was not late yet.

I had changed future state without changing their information.

Worse.

Lower lead continued.

“If I had known at second bell, I would have shifted four people to old-stake pull and kept only two bundling until we knew whether the wagon returned.”

That was a work-method choice.

His.

Exactly.

I had removed the information he needed to make it.

“I should have told you first.”

“You should have told all affected leads.”

“All?”

“Middle uses lower turnout path for basket return after fourth bell.”

I closed eyes.

Of course.

Shared route.

I had updated the vehicle.

Updated receiving crew.

Updated office.

Not updated every person whose local plan touched the route.

Old support memory arrived too late.

Changing one resource could change six people's timing without changing any of their orders.

“I need field steward.”

“He is at North.”

“Of course he is.”

Lower lead did not smile.

Cruel man.

We went to lower turnout.

Cut brush had been bundled along one side of access.

Not catastrophic.

But enough that a cart turning through would lose room.

Middle's basket return could still pass by hand.

A loaded cart would be annoying.

I did not decide whether annoying was acceptable.

Field steward did.

He arrived after runner found him.

Looked at brush.

Looked at road.

Looked at me.

“Why did Lower keep cutting?”

“Because I did not notify them when wagon priority changed.”

Lower lead said nothing.

Good.

No rescue.

Field steward asked, “Current wagon?”

“North turnout first. Lower after if time.”

“North brush stack size?”

“Unknown to me.”

“You sent wagon there without knowing?”

“House priority note ordered North first.”

He took note.

Read.

“Fine. That is not your decision.”

Good.

“But affected crew notification is.”

“Yes.”

He looked at lower turnout again.

“Stop adding brush here. Lower lead?”

“Yes.”

“Your people can move to old-stake pull west edge until fourth bell. Keep two on ditch cleanup if you want. Your method.”

“Accepted.”

There.

Not Greg assignment.

Field steward opened section.

Crew lead chose work split.

I updated.

Then Middle.

I found Middle lead before he found me.

Small mercy.

“Contract wagon changed to North first. Lower brush is staying in turnout longer. Field steward has stopped additional brush stacking there. Does that change your basket return?”

He looked toward lower road.

“Yes, because our return line uses the inside bend, and if those bundles creep another half pace we have either single-file carriers or we go around the stone wall, which is not far unless you are carrying wet spoil and then suddenly distance becomes a philosophical problem.”

“Current bundles are stopped.”

“Stopped where?”

“Lower turnout east edge.”

“Show me.”

We walked.

Well.

He walked.

I crutched.

He looked.

“Fine if they stay there.”

“Good.”

“Do they stay there?”

“Field steward stopped additional stacking.”

“Then yes.”

There.

Actual confirmation.

Not assumption.

I added:

**MIDDLE LEAD CONFIRMED basket return remains workable with current lower bundle position.**

Then I sent notice to North lead too.

She read.

“You changed wagon to us.”

“House did.”

“You knew.”

“Yes.”

“You told us.”

“Yes.”

“Then why are you here?”

“Because apparently I am learning notification is not finished until I know who change hurts.”

She looked at me.

“Expensive lesson?”

“Completion fee currently endangered only emotionally.”

She handed note back.

“Lower mad?”

“Formal.”

“Worse.”

“Yes.”

By third bell contract wagon reached North.

North brush stack actually did need clearing before evening house cart passage.

So priority change was not stupid.

Important.

Sometimes bad coordination came from bad instruction.

This was not that.

Instruction was valid.

My transmission was incomplete.

Wagon loaded North brush.

I did not supervise loading.

North lead and wagon people handled it.

I recorded departure.

At fourth bell wagon returned.

Lower had fewer new brush bundles because lead had shifted people exactly as he said he would have earlier.

They loaded what existed.

Not all planned brush moved.

Lower crew did not fail.

House priority had changed.

Record reflected that.

At fifth bell I went back to field office.

The woman read my day sheet.

Stopped at the priority change.

Read longer.

Then:

“Why is there an organizer-caused delay entry?”

“Because I caused one.”

“How long?”

“Lower crew continued old brush plan for about half a bell after priority changed because I failed to notify them. No worker idle time established. It created excess brush at lower turnout and required field-steward reassignment before the expected wagon window.”

She looked up.

“You could have written priority transition delay.”

“That would be true.”

“And shorter.”

“It would also hide who failed.”

She tapped paper.

“The house does not need confession. It needs useful record.”

Fair.

“What is useful wording?”

She thought.

“Priority change received before second bell. Wagon reassigned North. Lower crew notification delayed approximately half bell by organizer. Lower continued prior plan until notified. Field steward reassigned allowable work. No injury. No worker idle period recorded. Lower brush haul reduced.”

I wrote it.

Better.

Factual.

Less theatrical guilt.

“Do I lose completion?”

“Not from that.”

“Good.”

“If you do it again, maybe.”

“Less good.”

She pointed at communication section.

“You have sender and receiver for wagon.”

“Yes.”

“Add affected-party acknowledgment for priority changes.”

There.

System change.

Not moral lesson.

I added a small column.

**AFFECTED LEADS ACKNOWLEDGED**

Annoying.

Useful.

Day three record accepted.

Still no completion money.

Six silver from the start term was already real. Twelve more remained conditional.

That night Lyssa was home before me.

Rare enough to be suspicious.

She had one foot on chair and was pulling thread from a seam with small blade.

“Bad day?”

“Educational.”

“That means bad.”

“I forgot to tell a crew I moved their wagon.”

“You moved their wagon?”

“House moved wagon. I moved information badly.”

She pulled another stitch.

“Did anybody die?”

“No.”

“Did anybody lose money?”

“Not established.”

“Did anybody yell?”

“No.”

“That sounds fake.”

“The Lower lead was formal.”

“Oh.”

She understood.

I ate.

Told her the useful part.

Not every cart.

Not every section.

Just that I had updated the schedule everywhere except one of the people whose work depended on it.

Lyssa said, “That sounds like you.”

“Hostile home environment.”

“You like systems more than people sometimes.”

I opened mouth.

Closed it.

She looked pleased.

“Terrible woman.”

“Yes.”

Fourth day came with rain.

Not hard.

Enough to turn edges dark and make every road decision slightly more expensive.

Field steward kept all three sections open but marked Lower drainage for shorter checks.

His decision.

North crew arrived nine instead of ten.

Middle seven.

Lower eight.

Meal count twenty-four.

I changed roster.

Changed provisioning count.

Both.

Growth.

Cart A had twenty-four meal portions.

I nearly became arrogant.

Then did not.

Cart B arrived on time.

Contract wagon had no fourth-day assignment because the house priority sheet moved final brush haul to its own evening cart.

Good.

Fewer moving parts.

I still used affected-lead acknowledgment column when field steward shortened Lower's work window.

Lower lead signed initial after I told him.

Middle lead initialed when basket-return route changed by one path because rain softened the lower bend.

North lead refused to initial.

“Why?”

“I heard you.”

“Office wants acknowledgment.”

“Then write I heard you.”

“That is acknowledgment.”

“Then why do I need to write?”

I considered.

She was right enough.

The office had told me to add affected-party acknowledgment.

Not necessarily signatures.

I wrote:

**NORTH LEAD verbally acknowledged 2nd-bell Cart A return change.**

Then showed her.

She read.

“Fine.”

Good.

No bureaucracy for its own sake.

By midday nothing dramatic had happened.

By afternoon even less.

North finished its contracted ditch segment.

Middle handed off the south access edge.

Lower completed the open section the steward had kept available and left the remaining wet edge marked for later house work outside these four days.

Not failure.

Scope.

Crew leads reported completion in their own terms.

I did not translate fieldcraft into my language.

I recorded handoffs.

North lead: section complete to marked post.

Middle lead: access line clear to agreed south edge, root crown at final marker left for house removal because it sat outside their contracted line.

Lower lead: drainage cut complete through open section; wet-turn edge excluded under steward hold.

Field steward signed readiness/handoff.

Tool keeper closed issue sheet.

Two long ditch hooks returned.

Basket count still nine at North.

Nobody had invented the missing three.

Good.

Cart A final water count closed.

Meal count closed.

Contract wagon had no unresolved route.

I brought four days of organizer records to field office.

The woman read them.

All of them.

This took time.

I sat.

Did not count future copper.

Tried not to.

Failed.

Ten copper.

If paid.

Twenty-two plus ten.

Thirty-two.

That was more liquid copper than I had held at once in a while.

Not silver.

Not rich.

But the old thirty-copper reserve marker lived there.

I stopped.

Not mine yet.

She kept reading.

Day one.

Two corrections.

Day two.

Meal count mismatch.

Day three.

Organizer notification delay.

Day four.

Rain route acknowledgment.

She tapped day three.

“Lower lead complain?”

“Not formally.”

“Did you ask?”

“Yes. He said record was accurate after correction.”

“Field steward?”

“Signed.”

She checked.

Then day four.

“Why no North lead initial?”

“Verbal acknowledgment. She objected to signing something when office only needed proof she received change.”

The woman looked at me.

“She objected?”

“Yes.”

“And you changed method?”

“I recorded verbal acknowledgment in front of her.”

“That is fine.”

Good.

She stacked papers.

“Accepted.”

I waited.

She looked amused.

“Four-day handoff accepted.”

There.

“Completion fee?”

“Still twelve silver.”

“Important question.”

She opened cash box.

Counted.

Twelve silver.

Put it on table.

I counted again.

Not because I distrusted her.

Because money deserved witnesses.

Twelve.

No conversion.

No celebration.

Just an eighteen-silver organizer term completed exactly as written.

She said, “You did adequately.”

“High praise.”

“You missed one affected crew on a priority change.”

“Yes.”

“You corrected without arguing that technically the schedule was updated.”

“I considered arguing internally.”

“I can tell.”

“Useful skill.”

“No.”

She slid my copy of accepted term over.

“Keep that. It is a reference.”

That mattered almost as much as copper.

Almost.

“What does it support?”

“Four-day organizer term completed with accepted records.”

“Field competence?”

“No.”

“Hiring?”

“No.”

“Safety?”

“No.”

“Beautiful.”

“You are strange.”

“Reference can include that?”

“No.”

Fair.

I folded paper carefully.

No promise of another contract.

No permanent position.

No crew became mine.

North lead would go wherever North crew went.

Middle lead would continue explaining material reality until language surrendered.

Lower lead would remain formal enough to make mistakes hurt more.

Field office would hire someone else next time if someone better existed.

Good.

The work had still happened.

At home I put twelve silver on table.

Lyssa looked at it.

Then me.

“How much?”

“Twelve.”

“For today?”

“Completion half. Eighteen silver for the four-day organizer term total.”

“That sounds better.”

“It is.”

She stopped with cup halfway to mouth.

Not dramatic.

Just noticed.

“Plus Vale?”

“Vale is the opposite direction.”

“Right.”

Vale still existed.

There it was.

For the first time, the existence of that account did not feel larger than my entire life.

I had enough independent earning power to stop guessing what I owed and finally reconcile the whole ugly thing.

Work limb still existed.

Other obligations might exist.

Bits existed.

Food existed.

Tomorrow existed.

The silver did not mean Vale was free to leave.

It meant I could finally look at old numbers without assuming every answer was no.

That was different.

Lyssa said, “Are you going to hand Antonius all of it tomorrow and come home proud and broke?”

“No.”

“Good.”

“I am going to verify what I actually owe first.”

She narrowed eyes.

“Who are you?”

“Growth is frightening.”

“Very.”

I put the copper away.

Did not separate twenty-three.

Did not pay anything.

Not yet.

First verify.

Vale.

Work limb.

Anything else actually contractual.

Not favors.

Not meals.

Not people being kind to me.

Real obligations only.

Then preserve enough cash that clearing the past did not destroy the future.

That thought wanted to become a manifesto.

I refused.

My right leg hurt.

My hands were tired.

One crutch tip had collected South Road mud in the outer groove.

I cleaned it with an old rag.

Much better use of evening.

Magic remained fifty-nine, fifty-three, one-forty-seven.

Hark & Venn had not sent word.

No theatre runner.

No artifact.

No sudden opportunity.

Eighteen silver earned across the organizer term.

Vale still open and due for reconciliation.

Operating reserve intact.

A completed organizer reference folded with my papers.

And one management lesson I trusted because it had cost somebody else half a bell of bad information.

A plan was not shared because I had written the current version.

It was shared when the people whose choices depended on it actually had it.

Obvious.

Expensive.

Mine now.

Tomorrow I could start asking which old obligations were real.

Tonight I cleaned mud off my crutch and ate.

That was enough.
# CHAPTER 487

## THE REPAYER

I had been avoiding one number by looking at smaller numbers.

That was impressive because I liked numbers.

Money did that.

South Road had paid better than the kind of work I had been taking before. Not rich. Not life changing. Enough silver that my purse had stopped sounding like a child's toy when I moved.

That should have felt good.

Instead it reminded me Antonius Vale owned a ledger with my name in it.

Not owned me.

Important distinction.

Felt less important before breakfast.

Lyssa was working at table with dark blue fabric, scissors, thread, and the expression she used when cloth had personally disappointed her.

I counted silver once.

Then again.

Not because count changed.

Because I was deciding how much I could remove without making myself stupid again.

Old Greg had a recurring financial strategy.

**Future Greg will solve it.**

Future Greg had filed complaint.

"Money face," Lyssa said.

"You still maintain I have one."

"Several."

"How many?"

"This one is bad."

Useful taxonomy.

I separated operating reserve first.

Not tiny copper floor anymore.

Enough silver for food, travel, records, broken crutch parts, opportunities, and one decision I had not predicted.

Then I separated eighteen silver.

Lyssa looked at stack.

"Vale."

"Maybe."

"Why maybe?"

"Because I am done paying remembered numbers."

She put scissors down.

"You verify."

"Exactly."

"Then pay?"

"If number is real."

She looked at eighteen silver.

"All?"

"No."

That was the problem.

I did not actually know.

Antonius had told me balances before. I had worked. Paid. Borrowed. Added costs. Financed the Tere gauge. Let him cover things I could not cover. Agreed to terms while wearing confidence from a life where silver had felt like pocket money.

I knew the account was ugly.

I had not made myself read the whole history in a while.

That was probably information.

I put eighteen silver in one pouch.

The rest stayed home.

Not because Antonius would rob me.

Because I might rob me.

Two crutches.

No liner.

No Hessa apparatus.

No artifact.

Just account.

Vale office was open by second bell.

Same front clerk.

Different stack of paper.

Commerce reproduced.

"Antonius?"

"In."

"Busy?"

"Yes."

"Can I annoy him while busy?"

"You usually do."

Progress.

A quarter bell later Antonius waved me in.

He looked at me.

Then the pouch.

Then me.

"No."

"I haven't asked."

"You are going to make payment dramatic."

"I was planning restrained competence."

"Worse."

I sat in guest chair.

Still uneven.

I rocked it once.

He stared.

"Continuity matters," I said.

"Fix it yourself."

"Then it stops being your chair."

"Excellent."

I put no money down.

That got attention.

"Full account first."

Antonius leaned back.

"You know you owe me."

"I know. I want the actual reconciled ledger. Principal. Advances. Tere. Fees. Interest. Payments. Work credits. Everything you consider collectible."

His expression changed.

Not surprise yet.

Interest.

"Why?"

"Because I have been treating the account like weather. I would like weather to have a number."

He called the clerk.

Not one ledger.

Three.

That was bad.

The clerk put them down carefully.

I stared.

"You said I had become less inconvenient."

"You have," Antonius said.

"This looks historical."

"It is."

Good.

We started at beginning.

Original advance.

Interest.

Second advance.

Third.

Payments.

Another advance.

Guild note.

Arlo materials.

Training cost Antonius had covered when I was convinced earning later was same as earning now.

Gambling stake his man had covered.

Fees.

Credits.

Work.

Tere gauge.

Five silver purchase principal.

Then the financing attached to it.

By the time the gauge line had become ten silver I had apparently decided this was evidence that I should borrow more carefully.

I had not.

More entries.

More interest.

Some waived penalties I had forgotten he waived.

Not interest.

Penalties.

Important difference.

Labor credits entered as agreed amounts.

Cash payments.

Credits from work that had been explicitly debt labor.

Separate paid work stayed separate.

The gauntlet appraisal had not been stolen into the debt account.

Good.

I had wondered.

The clerk turned final page.

There it was.

**ONE GOLD. SIX SILVER.**

I stared.

Then read it again.

Still one gold and six silver.

I looked at Antonius.

"That is real?"

"Yes."

"Collectible?"

"Yes."

"Not theoretical face balance with half of it something you would never enforce?"

"No."

I sat back.

Chair rocked.

Perfect.

"I'm dumb."

Antonius said, "In this area, yes."

"I knew thirty-five percent over eight days was bad."

"You argued about it."

"I knew repeated advances were worse."

"You requested them."

"I knew financing speculative equipment at short-term rates was stupid."

"You told me the equipment might be worth forty gold."

"That part might still be true."

"Then perhaps only financing was stupid."

"Thank you for precision."

He folded hands.

I looked down the ledger again.

One gold, six silver.

My old life had spent more than that without discussion.

That was probably the problem.

Silver had never felt emotionally large enough to me.

Gold had been money.

Platinum-tier resources had been real money.

Young Greg had inherited all of those instincts and none of the income.

"I thought I'd make more," I said.

Antonius shrugged.

"You eventually did."

"Not inside eight days."

"No."

"Repeatedly."

"Also no."

Cruel.

I tapped final balance.

"Did you actually expect me to pay this?"

He looked at me for longer than answer required.

"Not all of it."

There.

I laughed.

"Excellent."

"You asked."

"Why write interest you do not expect to collect?"

"I expect return."

"Different word."

"Intentionally."

I waited.

He continued.

"People who can borrow cheaply do not come to me for loans like yours. I take risks other lenders will not. Sometimes borrower repays. Sometimes business fails. Sometimes I get labor. Information. Introductions. First look. Access. Useful people remain reachable because they still have an account."

"A leash."

"If you prefer."

"You prefer leverage."

"Yes."

No apology.

Good.

At least honest.

"So you expected me to work for you forever."

"Forever is dramatic."

"Years."

"Possibly."

"And interest keeps that relationship alive."

"Often."

I stared.

"Predatory."

"Yes."

That stopped me more than defense would have.

"You are supposed to argue."

"Why?"

"So I can feel morally superior."

"You signed it."

Damn.

I looked at ledger.

"Any amount here you are waiving if I pay now?"

"No."

"Any friendship discount?"

"We are not friends."

"Good."

"Also no."

"Better."

That mattered.

I did not want release.

I wanted zero.

Different.

"Current payment terms?"

Antonius said, "Cash accepted. Work credit only when agreed in advance. No fixed installment. No invented penalty for missing a schedule that does not exist. I prefer surplus payment over payment that makes you unable to remain operational."

Same principle.

Larger number.

"Any minimum?"

"No."

"Any reason not to pay eighteen silver today?"

His eyebrows moved.

Tiny.

Real.

"How much do you have left if you do?"

"Enough."

"Number."

"Operating reserve in silver at home. Food. Fare. Records. Ordinary copper and bits."

"Work limb?"

"Separate. Nothing due today unless Hark & Venn says otherwise."

"Good."

"I hate when you say that."

"Pay eighteen."

Cruel.

I opened pouch.

Eighteen silver.

The first time I had paid Antonius, one copper had felt like proof debt could shrink.

This was not proof.

This was weight.

Coins actually sounded different at this amount.

Clerk counted.

Antonius counted only enough to annoy me.

Receipt written.

The account remained gold-denominated.

The clerk entered the eighteen-silver credit without translating the entire remaining balance into a fake number for my convenience.

Good.

I did not need a universal currency lecture.

I needed evidence that line moved.

It moved.

"Still ugly," I said.

"Yes."

"Good."

Antonius looked at me.

"Why good?"

"Because if I make this easy in my head, I will do it again."

"You will do something else stupid instead."

"Likely."

"Better."

I folded receipt.

"I am paying all of it."

There.

That got more reaction than eighteen silver.

Not much.

Antonius was Antonius.

But he stopped moving.

"Why?"

"Because I owe it."

"That is not usually enough reason to destroy useful liquidity."

"I am not destroying liquidity."

"Then when you have surplus."

"Yes."

"No deadline?"

"No invented deadline."

"Good."

"Stop saying good."

"No."

I stood.

Then stopped.

"Hark & Venn."

Antonius sighed.

"I am not their clerk."

"Correct. I am checking their clerk next."

"Then why tell me?"

"Conversation."

"Leave."

I left.

Vale account still open.

Eighteen silver credited.

Operating reserve intact.

No fake deadline.

No forgiveness.

No moral revelation.

Just a larger problem finally shaped correctly.

Hark & Venn shop smelled like wood dust, oil, leather, and enough metal filings to season soup.

Bad soup.

Another shop worker looked up.

"Greg."

Known enough.

"That concerning?"

"You come often enough."

"I aspire to be forgettable."

"Failed."

Good.

"Account question."

"Fit?"

"Money."

Worse word.

Older bookkeeper came from back.

No name needed.

I gave quote copy and deposit receipt.

"I am not here to pay unless account says payment is currently due. I need exact status."

Bookkeeper read.

Then pulled shop order.

Actual paper.

Good.

"Quote still active."

"One silver eighteen copper."

"Yes."

"Deposit twenty copper received."

"Yes."

"Applied?"

"Yes."

"What is due today?"

"Nothing scheduled today."

There.

"Final balance timing?"

"On final acceptance unless shop and customer agree otherwise."

"Final acceptance means completed work presented, fit accepted for release, account settled or alternate payment agreement made?"

"Yes."

"Completed work presented?"

"No."

"Then no payment due."

"No."

Excellent.

"Storage fee?"

"No."

"New fitting fee?"

"No. Existing order."

"Materials change affecting quote?"

Bookkeeper checked.

"No approved price change."

Good.

Not forever guaranteed.

Current.

"Can I make voluntary payment early?"

"Yes."

Could.

Different from should.

"What would early payment change?"

"Account balance."

"Production timing?"

"No."

"Material priority?"

"No."

"Fit schedule?"

"No."

Information.

"Then I am done."

Mara came through back doorway carrying leather strap and pencil.

"You're here."

"Apparently."

"Problem?"

"No."

She looked at bookkeeper.

"Money question."

Mara looked at me.

"Did you get rich?"

"No."

"Then stop paying people early."

"Hostile."

"Accurate."

"I paid Vale eighteen silver."

That got a pause.

"Why?"

"Because account is worse than I remembered."

"How much?"

"Enough."

"Greg."

"One gold six silver before today's credit."

She stared.

Then said, "You're stupid."

"Already established."

"Good."

Everyone.

"Your shop could have some money too."

"No."

"Bookkeeper says I can."

"Can is not should."

"Conspiracy."

She pointed pencil at me.

"Not until it changes something."

Then disappeared back.

That was Hark & Venn update.

No fitting.

No secret completion.

No dramatic work limb under cloth.

Just account.

Useful.

Outside I wrote:

**VALE: full account verified. 1g6s before today's credit. Paid 18s. No waiver. No fixed schedule. Pay surplus, remain operational.**

Then:

**H&V: quote unchanged 1s18c. 20c deposit received/applied. Nothing scheduled due today. Final balance due on final acceptance unless alternate agreement. Early payment allowed but changes only account balance.**

I stopped at public fountain because pouch strap was annoying me.

Not painful.

Annoying.

Important category.

A boy beside fountain watched me.

Maybe ten.

Wooden hoop.

"Did you lose your leg in war?"

"No."

"Monster?"

"No."

"Cart?"

"No."

He frowned.

"What then?"

"Badly."

He considered that.

"That's not a thing."

"It was at the time."

His mother called.

He ran away dissatisfied.

Good.

I checked pouch strap.

One stitch stretched.

Retied through second loop.

Money stayed where I wanted it.

Body stayed where I wanted it.

Mostly.

The route home could have passed Vale again.

I did not take it.

Not because temptation to pay more.

Because I had already made decision.

Repeating decision every street corner was not discipline.

It was anxiety wearing spectacles.

I bought onions with bits.

A woman selling lamp wick claimed new batch burned twice as long.

"Compared to what?"

"Old batch."

"Whose old batch?"

"Mine."

"Tested?"

She stared.

I bought onions and left wick.

Apparently Hessa had colonized shopping too.

At one crossing a porter dropped a bundle of reed slats.

People helped because slats blocked road.

I could not help much without surrendering both hands and becoming furniture.

So I held one rolling slat with crutch tip and let people with free hands do actual work.

Porter said thanks.

"My contribution was preventing one stick."

"Important stick."

"Best one."

Then kept going.

No lesson.

No job.

No commission.

City afternoon.

That mattered.

Eighteen silver had just left my life and the day had not narrowed around it.

I still bought onions.

Still took longer route.

Still had enough reserve to make another decision tomorrow.

That was progression.

Not debt virtue.

Not austerity.

Just capacity.

At home Lyssa was back.

She looked at receipt.

"Big."

"Yes."

"Still owe."

"Yes."

"You pay all?"

"Eventually."

"Why?"

I thought about Antonius admitting he did not really expect perfect cash collection.

About leverage.

About being useful enough that a creditor might prefer account to remain open.

About how tempting that flexibility could become.

"Because I want it finished," I said.

Lyssa nodded.

"Not today."

"No."

"Good."

Everyone had joined conspiracy.

I put receipt with older Vale papers.

Not trophy.

Evidence.

Then I ate onions with dinner and discovered they were sharper than expected.

Some risks remained impossible to price.

Before bed I wrote one last line.

**Do not pay debt by making yourself unable to earn. Also stop borrowing like old Greg has young Greg's income.**

That was enough.

The account was large.

Finite.

Mine.

And for the first time in a while, I actually intended to kill it.
# CHAPTER 488

## THE ACTOR

Twenty copper lasted through breakfast.

This was less impressive than thirty-two.

It was also more useful than nine.

I decided not to improve it before noon.

Dangerous experiment.

Lyssa had already left for work.

The room was quiet except for street carts, somebody arguing about onions downstairs, and one pigeon that had developed a personal grievance against the sill.

I ate bread.

Used the last of yesterday's onions.

Did not calculate return on onions.

Growth.

Vale eleven.

Hark & Venn nothing due.

Magic fifty-nine, fifty-three, one-forty-seven.

No South Road contract.

No buyer.

No seller.

No one waiting for me to fix movement of anything.

I had become temporarily unemployed in four separate disciplines.

Excellent.

The theatre runner found me before second bell.

Not the same visitor from before.

Actual theatre runner.

Young man, narrow shoulders, damp hair, carrying three folded notices and breathing like he had decided stairs were political.

"Greg?"

"Unfortunately."

"Rinna says come."

"Why?"

"She said not to explain because you'd ask questions."

I looked at him.

"That's insulting."

"She was right."

Strong runner.

I took crutches.

No bag beyond notebook.

No money pouch beyond bits and two copper because leaving home with nothing had become unnecessary performance.

The theatre smelled like dust, glue, old cloth, and somebody boiling something that should not have been boiled indoors.

Home-adjacent.

Rinna stood near stage with script in one hand.

Nella sat on edge of platform wearing rehearsal trousers and one shoe.

The other shoe was beside her.

I pointed.

"Loss?"

"Choice."

"Concerning."

"It hurts."

"Less concerning."

Rinna held script toward me.

"No."

"I haven't asked."

"You came holding pages."

"That is not consent."

"Read."

There it was.

I took pages.

Not prompt copy.

Scene.

Actual scene.

Five pages.

My role marked **HARROW**.

I knew Harrow.

Not personally.

Character.

Older younger brother.

Which was already annoying phrase.

The play had been in rehearsal while I traveled. I had seen pieces before leaving and bits when I substituted prompt-side after returning.

Nella played Mara Vale.

Not Vale related to Antonius.

Probably.

Different Vale.

Need not investigate.

Harrow was her brother, recently home after six years away, pretending he had come back because their father was sick when he had actually come back because the river company had collapsed and taken his money.

Good.

Normal family disaster.

"Where is Pell?" I asked.

"Sick," Rinna said.

"Renn?"

"Back."

Good.

One uncertainty resolved casually.

Renn was apparently alive and working again.

No ceremony.

"Why me?"

"Because you know scene traffic, you're here, and Nella needs another body with enough words to run the second half."

"Enough words."

"Do not become proud."

Nella said, "Pell does it better."

"Thank you."

"He does."

"I believed first time."

She looked at me.

Good.

Not everyone cushioning ego.

Rinna tapped page.

"This is rehearsal. You are not replacing Pell. Pell is still Harrow unless illness grows ambition. We need Nella's scene. You read Harrow."

"How much acting?"

"Some."

"Terrible unit."

"More than table read. Less than costume."

Useful.

I put crutches at side of stage.

That created immediate problem.

Harrow crossed from window to center table, then to door, then back.

I did not.

Current me had two crutches.

No trial limb.

No theatrical miracle.

Rinna watched me look at blocking marks.

"Adapt."

"Authority?"

"Acting blocking for this rehearsal only. Do not redesign scene."

There.

I moved chair closer to center line.

Kept one crutch against it.

Other stayed under right hand.

Could stand, shift, sit, turn.

Not cross quickly.

Harrow would become less mobile in this run.

Fine.

Nella put second shoe back on.

Apparently pain had negotiated.

We started.

Scene opened with her folding father's shirts.

Harrow entered.

My first line:

"I thought you would have burned those."

I said it.

Correctly.

Nothing happened.

Nella looked at me.

In character maybe.

Then said her line.

"He still wears them."

I said, "He still thinks he does."

Good line.

I liked it.

I said it like I liked it.

Rinna stopped us.

"No."

"What?"

"You're showing us line."

"I spoke line."

"You presented it."

Nella said, "You made face before it."

"I have face."

"Yes."

Rinna pointed at start.

"Again. Harrow has been in house ten minutes. He knows father is worse than letter said. He is trying not to let Mara ask why he came home. Stop acting like audience deserves warning when good sentence arrives."

Cruel.

Accurate.

Again.

"I thought you would have burned those."

"He still wears them."

"He still thinks he does."

Better.

Not much.

Nella folded shirt.

She did not look up.

Her next three lines were longer than mine.

She spoke while folding.

Not cleanly.

Character thought changed halfway through.

"Mrs. Pell says he asks for tea and then forgets why it's there, and yesterday he told me Mother would be angry if I left the window open, which would be interesting if Mother had not been dead nine years, and I shut it anyway because I was tired."

The line landed because Nella did not polish it.

She sounded tired.

Actually tired.

I forgot next line.

Not entirely.

It existed somewhere.

Prompt-side instinct looked for cue copy that was not there.

Renn whispered from side:

"Then why write me?"

Right.

I said, "Then why write me?"

Late.

Nella looked up.

"Because I wanted you home."

That was scene.

Simple.

My next line was supposed to be:

"You wanted help."

I said it too fast.

Rinna stopped.

"No."

I looked at page.

"It's four words."

"Yes."

"Useful."

"Not when you use them to escape."

Nella said, "You sound like Harrow is cleverer than her."

"He thinks he is."

"Not there."

I looked at her.

She pointed at page.

"She just said she wanted him home. He doesn't know what to do with that. Pell lets it sit."

Pell.

Better actor.

Good.

"What do you do?" I asked.

Nella frowned.

"When?"

"As Mara. After saying it."

"Nothing."

"Nothing?"

"Yes."

She demonstrated.

"Because I wanted you home."

Then she just looked at me.

No gesture.

No cleverness.

Uncomfortable.

I understood.

Hated it.

Again.

"Then why write me?"

"Because I wanted you home."

Silence.

Longer.

Not theatre-long.

Human-long.

I felt impulse to fill it.

Joke.

Move.

Look away.

Harrow probably felt same.

Good.

"You wanted help."

This time it came smaller.

Nella's answer:

"I did too."

There.

Better.

Rinna did not stop.

We continued.

Harrow tried to make father practical.

Meals.

Doctor.

Money.

Roof.

Mara refused to let him turn return into maintenance contract.

Good scene.

I liked play more now.

At page three, Harrow crossed to door in original blocking.

I could not make that distance smoothly while holding pages and using crutch.

I tucked pages under arm.

Bad.

Lost place.

Rinna stopped.

"Pages on table."

"Then I can't see line at door."

"Don't go door."

"Blocking says door."

"Rehearsal says current body."

That was simple.

Nella said, "Pell goes door because he wants to leave."

"I also want leave."

"Then make me believe it from chair."

Hostile craft.

Good.

I sat.

Harrow's next line was:

"I can send money."

Mara:

"From where?"

Then Harrow lied.

"North office kept me."

Important.

I said lie too smoothly.

Nella laughed.

Out of character.

"That is Greg lie."

"What?"

"You say bad thing like you've already prepared defense."

"I have experience."

"Exactly."

Rinna said, "Harrow hasn't practiced this lie enough."

Interesting.

I tried again.

"I can send money."

"From where?"

"North office kept me."

Too hesitant.

Rinna shook head.

"Now he's twelve."

"Useful spectrum."

"Find middle."

I did.

Three more times.

Not exciting.

Third was worse than second.

Fourth finally had tiny break between North and office.

Like Harrow selected lie while speaking.

Nella's face changed.

She heard it.

"Kept you doing what?"

I answered.

"Accounts."

"Whose?"

"River."

"Which river?"

There.

Character trapped.

I smiled.

Rinna stopped.

"Why are you smiling?"

"Good trap."

"Greg is enjoying writing. Harrow is losing."

Right.

Again.

No smile.

Harder than magic.

Magic at least did not care about expression.

Scene pushed Harrow toward admitting company failed.

He still did not admit money.

Mara knew anyway.

Nella had one line:

"You came home poor and decided shame would be less visible if you carried groceries."

Excellent.

I laughed.

Everyone stopped.

Nella stared.

"That is my line."

"I know."

"Then stop appreciating it."

"Good line."

Rinna said, "Audience can appreciate it. Harrow cannot."

"I disagree."

"Harrow is being disemboweled."

"Metaphorically."

"Act like it."

Again.

This time line hit.

"You came home poor and decided shame would be less visible if you carried groceries."

I felt stupidly seen.

Not because exact.

Because mechanism.

Come back useful enough and maybe nobody asks what failed.

That thought did not belong only Harrow.

Dangerous.

I did not use it as revelation.

I let it make eye contact harder.

Nella saw change.

She kept going.

Good actor.

"Did you think Father would care?"

"I didn't come for him."

First true line.

Nella stopped folding.

"Mara knows that?" I asked.

Rinna said nothing.

Nella said, "She does now."

We ran rest.

Scene ended without reconciliation.

Mara handed Harrow one of father's shirts.

He took it.

Not hug.

Not forgiveness.

Just object.

Harrow said:

"This won't fit me."

Mara:

"I know."

Blackout.

Good.

Rinna said, "Again from 'You came home poor.'"

No praise.

Excellent.

Then again.

By fourth run, my shoulder started complaining from repeated stand-sit with crutch.

Not pain.

Work.

Better.

Different.

Good boundary.

Good.

"Good."

Interesting.

Good.

My pause belongs to me.

Annoying repetition across life.

Sick enough to look offended by air.

Not because perfect.

Because Rinna wanted whole shape.

Nella stepped on one line.

A chair leg caught hem.

Renn dropped something backstage.

At "You came home poor," I did not think about my own money.

At least not first.

I thought about Harrow.

That was probably acting.

At final shirt exchange, Nella handed it to me.

"This won't fit me."

"I know."

I held shirt.

No blackout because rehearsal.

Silence.

Rinna closed script.

"Fine."

High praise.

"How fine?"

"Enough."

Nella sat and removed painful shoe immediately.

I pointed.

"Victory."

"Blister."

"Less poetic."

"Better."

"No."

She frowned.

"What?"

"You worked half day."

"You asked read."

"That is work."

There.

Old mistake.

Thinking theatre participation became gift if informal.

No.

Labor.

"Fine."

Cash twenty-one.

Vale eleven.

No debt payment.

Good.

"No," Rinna said.

"Excellent."

"Everyone committed to clarity."

Outside the theatre, evening traffic had thickened around the market turn. I waited for a handcart to clear instead of trying to angle both crutches through the narrowing gap. The driver apologized after he had already blocked everything.

"No injury."

"Still sorry."

"Accepted."

He moved.

I moved.

Nobody wrote it down.

That felt almost luxurious after South Road.

My hands were tired from the rehearsal more than I expected. Not from carrying. From standing, sitting, pages, crutch, shirt, chair, repeated resets. Acting apparently had logistics too.

Of course it did.

On way home I spent one bit on hot bread.

Not because income.

Because bread was hot.

Important distinction.

"Acting."

"Same question."

She knew play enough.

"Yes."

"No."

"What?"

"I didn't."

"You did."

"Everyone is director."

"Less bad."

"That sounds believable."

"Good."

No accounting.

"Working bad thread."

"Not same as good."

Hessa had colonized sewing too.

"Yes."

"Because you talk during pauses."

Cruel.

Accurate.

Did not make one.

Lyssa smiled.

There.

Twenty-one copper.

Eleven Vale.

Bits unspecified.

Magic unchanged.

Work limb unchanged.

No deal.

No organizer contract.

No artifact.

Pell was sick but still Harrow.

Nella was better actor than me.

Not excellent.

Not secretly brilliant.

Not transformed.

That was plenty.

Tomorrow could become complicated again.

Tonight there was hot bread and bad thread and Lyssa deliberately leaving a pause open after I had just learned not to fill one.

"What?"

She laughed.

Failure remained available.

Again.

# CHAPTER 490

## THE CONTRACTOR

The South Road reference arrived before the work did.

That felt backward.

A folded copy sat under our door with the field office stamp, my name spelled correctly, and one sentence beneath the four-day term record.

**Completed organizer term with accepted daily records.**

That was all.

No praise.

No poetry.

No claim I understood drainage.

Perfect.

Lyssa read it while standing because sitting had apparently become optional in her profession.

"That is very boring."

"High compliment."

"It says you finished."

"Exactly."

"It does not say you were good."

"Excellent reference."

She handed it back.

I had real silver now.

Not rich.

Not safe forever.

Enough that I no longer needed to count every copper like it had emotional significance.

Vale still existed.

That mattered more.

Eighteen silver had already gone into that account.

The remaining balance still sat on Antonius's ledger in mixed gold and silver terms I was deliberately not converting in my head because currency conversion was a real market activity, not a personality trait.

Magic remained fifty-nine, fifty-three, one-fifty-nine.

Hark & Venn had nothing due.

One boring reference.

That was enough to change morning.

A runner arrived before second bell.

Not theatre.

Different clothes.

Merchant-house badge on shoulder.

"Greg?"

"Yes."

"South Road organizer?"

"For four days."

"Good enough."

Dangerous sentence.

He handed me a note.

**WEST MARKET RECEIVING HOUSE**

**ONE-DAY COORDINATION CONTRACT**

**THREE INBOUND WAGONS / TWO RECEIVING CREWS / ONE CERTIFIED SCALE / CLOSE OF RECEIVING AT SIXTH BELL**

**CURRENT DISPATCH CLERK ILL**

**REFERENCE REQUIRED**

**9 SILVER ON ACCEPTED CLOSE RECORD**

I read twice.

Nine silver.

One day.

That was not theatre money.

That was not clerical side work.

That was a house deciding a day of coordinated failure would cost it enough to pay for prevention.

Good.

"Why me?"

Runner shrugged.

"Field office sent three names. You were closest."

Excellent.

Not destiny.

Geography.

"Who owns decisions?"

He blinked.

"What?"

"Loading, scale acceptance, storage placement, damaged goods, late arrival. Who decides each?"

He looked at note like answers might appear if threatened.

"Receiving master."

"All?"

"Mostly."

Bad word.

"Take me there."

West Market receiving house occupied a broad yard behind two warehouses and one narrow office that looked structurally offended by paperwork.

Three marked wagon bays.

One scale platform.

Two receiving crews.

One warehouse door wide enough for exactly one cart if everyone had behaved.

No one had.

A woman at yard board saw my crutches, saw note, and said, "You're the field boy."

"Temporary organizer."

"Same problem."

"Different dirt."

She almost smiled.

Receiving master.

Good.

I showed South Road reference.

She read one line.

"Accepted records."

"Yes."

"Four days."

"Yes."

"Today is one."

"Promising."

She pointed at yard board.

Three inbound wagons:

North kiln pigment.

East cloth rolls.

South lamp oil.

Normal commerce.

That mattered.

No artifacts.

No contraband.

No reason for the day to become interesting except commerce was perfectly capable of doing that alone.

The house had one certified scale because cloth did not require full weight certification if seals matched, while pigment and oil did.

Crew One handled dry goods.

Crew Two handled casks and liquids.

Warehouse space:

Dry room west.

Cloth rack upper.

Oil cellar rear through lower ramp.

Simple.

Then she explained current problem quickly enough to become weather.

Pigment due before third bell.

Cloth due at third.

Oil between third and fourth.

Oil had scale priority once physically present because cellar window closed first.

South lane had to be clear by fifth for cooper empties.

Crew One had six.

Crew Two had four because two were out.

I waited.

She stopped.

"Again slowly."

She stared.

"You're organizer."

"Yes. I organize facts after receiving them."

Second version was better.

I wrote.

Then authority.

"Scale certification?"

"Scale clerk."

"Seal mismatch?"

"Me."

"Damaged cask?"

"Cooper lead for containment. Me for acceptance."

"Storage placement?"

"Warehouse lead."

"Unload method?"

"Crew leads."

"Late wagon?"

"Me if receiving remains open. Office manager if penalty question."

Good.

My authority:

arrival order.

approved bay assignment.

crew notice.

scale queue.

handoff timestamps.

current-state board.

Nothing about rejecting goods.

Nothing about opening sealed cloth.

Nothing about deciding whether oil was safe.

Good.

"Why nine silver?"

Receiving master looked at me.

"Because our dispatch clerk is sick and the house has three deliveries worth enough that I do not care about nine silver if the yard closes cleanly."

There.

Real scale.

"And because?"

She narrowed eyes.

"And because if oil misses cellar window we pay hold, crew time, and probably a seller argument I do not want."

"Useful."

"Do not make me price my own headache for you."

"Fair."

Accepted close record meant all three lots either received into assigned storage or held/rejected under receiving-master decision, with arrival, scale, crew, and handoff recorded.

If seller failed to arrive, not my failure.

If load arrived and house lost it inside its own yard, potentially mine.

Good distinction.

I signed.

No start payment.

No guarantee of future work.

Nine silver on accepted close.

First obvious problem:

Board had contract windows.

No live expected times.

South Road had already taught me scheduled state and actual state were different animals.

"Runner contact for all three?"

"Yes."

"Current estimates?"

"No."

"Let's get them."

Receiving master sent runners.

Her people.

Her authority.

I made three columns.

**CONTRACT WINDOW**

**LATEST REPORTED POSITION**

**YARD STATE**

Pigment runner returned first.

Left before first bell. Axle check at Tanner turn. Maybe half bell.

Cloth loaded, waiting city gate clearance.

Oil delayed because two casks had bad hoops and replacements were being loaded.

Important.

Oil later than planned.

Maybe still fine.

Third bell approached.

Pigment did not.

Cloth did.

Of course.

Cloth driver entered east gate already talking.

"I was told bay two, but bay two has handbarrows, and I can wait, obviously I can wait, except gate clerk wrote arrival before third and if your yard writes third my house says I lost time here, which I did, but mostly because the fish cart at south crossing had decided turning was a spiritual exercise."

Long speech.

Good.

"Arrival recorded. Bay not yet."

He stopped.

"Oh."

Crew One lead checked seals.

Matched.

No scale.

Bay two had barrows staged for pigment.

Current plan assumed pigment first.

Reality disagreed.

"Can cloth use bay one?"

Crew lead said yes.

Less direct to rack.

Still workable.

Receiving master approved.

I recorded.

Cloth moved.

Halfway through second roll, pigment arrived.

Scale free.

Oil absent.

Easy.

Crew One split itself.

Not me.

Two finish cloth.

Four pigment.

I updated board.

Oil runner returned.

Carrier at cooper crossing.

Fifth cask strap slipped.

No leak.

Quarter bell maybe.

Receiving master said still fine.

I wrote.

Pigment cleared scale.

Warehouse lead assigned west dry room.

Cloth finished.

Bay one clear.

Everything looked competent.

Danger.

Oil arrived just before fourth bell.

Five casks.

Crew Two ready.

Scale clear.

Then driver said, "One cask hoop was replaced after depot manifest."

Receiving master stopped.

"Which?"

Third cask.

No leak.

New outer hoop.

Seal plate intact.

I did not inspect.

Not my authority.

Receiving master and cooper lead did.

Cooper lead spoke slowly.

"Hoop new. Head dry. No active seep. Plate intact. Roll separately. Watch after scale."

Receiving master accepted conditional handling.

"Record."

I recorded.

Scale clerk weighed first two.

Third reached platform.

Scale clerk frowned.

"Mark doesn't match manifest weight."

There.

Driver immediately explained replacement cask had been topped from rejected one, depot clerk may have copied gross from old cask, everyone was hurrying, and apparently responsibility could be diluted by sentence length.

Receiving master held up hand.

"Stop."

Good.

Difference mattered.

Not giant.

Enough.

Cooper lead confirmed no leak.

Receiving master could isolate.

Decision:

third cask to hold bay three.

remaining two scale now.

That was her decision.

My lane was preventing disputed cask from occupying the one certified scale while paperwork argument happened.

"Move disputed cask to bay three under cooper hold. Scale four and five. Driver stays available."

Receiving master nodded.

Crew lead nodded.

Fourth.

Fifth.

Scale.

Lower ramp.

Cellar.

The disputed third sat in bay three looking exactly like a barrel.

Commerce.

Driver wanted to find depot clerk.

Receiving master sent runner instead and kept driver with load.

He argued long enough to become weather.

I let her own that too.

By fifth bell:

Pigment stored.

Cloth stored.

Four oil casks stored.

One held.

South lane clear for cooper empties.

Contract could close with written hold decision if correction never arrived.

Receiving master still wanted corrected manifest.

Good.

Fifth and quarter, runner returned.

Original manifest gross belonged rejected cask.

Replacement cask had been topped lower.

Corrected gross matched certified scale within accepted tolerance.

Scale clerk checked.

Receiving master signed correction.

Cooper lead checked cask again.

Still dry.

"Accept."

Third cask returned to scale because corrected paper and actual weight now agreed.

Then cellar.

Done before sixth bell.

Not dramatic.

Good work rarely was.

I assembled close record.

Cloth arrival.

Seal match.

No scale.

Crew One.

Upper rack.

Pigment arrival.

Scale.

Crew split approved by lead.

West dry room.

Oil arrival.

Casks one, two, four, five cleared and stored.

Cask three held pending discrepancy.

Replacement-hoop condition.

Corrected depot note.

Scale acceptance.

Cellar handoff.

No goods lost.

No unauthorized acceptance decision by me.

No safety decision by me.

Receiving master reviewed.

She changed one phrase.

I had written:

**cask three delayed due to incorrect manifest.**

She changed it to:

**cask three held pending discrepancy review.**

"Why?"

"Because incorrect was not established when hold began."

Hessa had infected commerce again.

"Fair."

She signed.

Accepted close record.

Office clerk counted nine silver onto table.

Nine.

One day.

I stared for less time than I would have months ago.

Still enough that clerk noticed.

"Problem?"

"No."

Receiving master said, "You expected less."

"I expected nine. I am adjusting to nine existing."

"Do it outside."

Good.

I took money.

Not wealth.

Not new permanent baseline.

A strong urgent contract.

But enough that Vale became a different kind of problem.

Not tiny.

Not gone.

Possible.

That was new.

I bought a meat pie with bits.

Then walked west.

Not directly to Vale.

First to a licensed moneychanger near merchant hall.

Important distinction.

I had silver.

Vale's remaining account was recorded across gold and silver.

I was not going to invent a universal exchange rate because I happened to be protagonist.

Moneychanger had current board, spread, fee, and enough boredom to make this normal.

"Need mixed payment," I said.

"Amount?"

I showed Vale account copy and the eighteen-silver credit receipt.

He read.

Looked at me.

"Vale."

"Unfortunately."

"Closing?"

"Yes."

That changed his attention slightly.

Not impressed.

Specific.

He calculated using current house exchange.

I did not memorize rate.

I cared about output.

He told me how much silver I needed to surrender to receive exact remaining mixed coin, less his fee.

I checked arithmetic on his written slip.

Then checked again.

No secret rate lesson.

No worldbuilding lecture.

Just a transaction.

I had enough.

More importantly, after exchange I would still have operating reserve.

Not early-book poverty.

Not empty.

Enough silver remained that food, fare, records, tools, and ordinary mistakes stayed possible.

I made exchange.

He counted exact mixed coin into one pouch.

Returned silver change into another.

I did not like how heavy first pouch felt.

That was probably healthy.

Vale office was almost on route home.

Almost.

Close enough that choosing it did not require another chapter.

Front clerk looked up.

"Antonius?"

"Busy."

"I don't need Antonius."

That felt new.

"What do you need?"

"Current account after last credit. Exact."

Ledger came.

Same history.

Same eighteen-silver payment.

No new fee.

No surprise interest invented between visits beyond what contract already established.

I compared moneychanger slip to Vale balance.

Matched.

I put pouch on counter.

"Close it."

Clerk looked at amount.

Then me.

"All?"

"All."

She counted.

Once.

Twice.

Called second clerk.

Third count.

Good.

Large enough to deserve boring redundancy.

Then she wrote receipt.

Stamped account.

**PAID / BALANCE ZERO**

I looked at words.

That was it.

No storm.

No revelation.

No morality.

One ugly contract completed exactly as written.

Antonius emerged anyway because universe disliked restraint.

He saw receipt.

Then the empty account line.

Then me.

He stopped.

That was more reaction than usual.

"Done?" I asked.

"Apparently."

"You sound surprised."

"I am."

There.

Better than applause.

"You thought I'd keep paying forever."

"I thought account would remain useful longer."

"Leash."

"If you insist."

"I do."

He looked at change pouch in my hand.

"How much did you keep?"

"Enough."

"Number."

"About twelve silver plus ordinary copper and bits after food and exchange fee."

He nodded once.

"Good."

"That is all?"

"What else?"

"I just paid one gold six silver worth of terrible decisions."

"You made the decisions."

"True."

"And paid them."

"Also true."

He looked at receipt again.

"That part I did not expect."

I smiled.

"There. Confetti."

"No."

Consistent.

"Need work?" he asked.

Old question.

Different shape.

I thought.

"Not today."

He nodded.

No offense.

No reminder that I owed him.

Because I did not.

I left.

Outside, city remained offensively normal.

Cart wheel squeaked.

Someone argued about onions.

A dog stole something flat and bread-shaped.

I stood under awning because right palm had started complaining about crutch pressure.

Not injury.

Ordinary work fatigue.

I shifted weight.

Flexed fingers.

Waited.

Earning more did not turn shoulder or hands into abstract concepts.

Good.

On way home I bought sour apples with bits because Lyssa liked sour things for reasons I considered hostile.

At home she saw pouch first.

Then apples.

"How much?"

"About twelve silver left, plus smaller coin."

She looked at me.

"Vale?"

"Zero."

Pause.

"All?"

"All."

Another pause.

"Good."

Apparently everybody in my life had conspired around one word.

I put apples down.

She bit one.

Made face.

"Too sour?"

"Good."

"You're all sick."

She offered me bite.

I refused because growth.

Later I opened notebook.

Old pages had too much copper in them.

Old thresholds.

Old tiny numbers treated like mountains because at the time they were mountains.

I did not erase them.

Context mattered.

I wrote:

**VALE: 0. CLOSED. FULL.**

Then:

**Reserve: about 12s + ordinary copper/bits. Keep operating room.**

Then stopped.

No new debt audit.

No attempt to optimize every obligation before sleep.

Hark & Venn would matter when work limb actually moved.

Magic would matter when Hessa had designed next protocol.

Theatre would exist whether profitable or not.

Lyssa was still going to argue about thread.

Some obligations disappeared.

Some arguments were permanent.

That seemed healthy.
